warmup.q: A worker thread runs while (!stop) { spins++; }. One second later, main sets the plain field stop = true. What happens on a normal JDK 25 run?
options: The worker stops within a few nanoseconds
The worker stops within a millisecond or so, once the CPU cache is flushed
warmup.why: The JIT compiler may read stop once, keep it in a register and turn the loop into while (true). Nothing in the code tells it another thread writes that field. The cache story in option 2 is the tempting one, but caches keep each other up to date on their own. The value that goes stale is the copy the compiled code keeps in a register.

sections.h: A plain boolean can keep a loop running forever
sections.html:
Here is the smallest version of a bug that ships in real services. A worker thread loops until another thread asks it to stop.

Java
static boolean stop;   // plain field

Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
    long spins = 0;
    while (!stop) {
        spins++;
    }
    System.out.println("worker saw stop");
});
worker.start();
Thread.sleep(1_000);
stop = true;           // main asks the worker to stop
Kotlin
var stop = false       // plain property

val worker = thread {
    var spins = 0L
    while (!stop) {
        spins++
    }
    println("worker saw stop")
}
Thread.sleep(1_000)
stop = true            // main asks the worker to stop

Run it on JDK 21 or 25 and the worker never stops. Not after a second, not after an hour. main wrote true, and the worker keeps reading false.

Now run the same program with java -Xint. That flag turns off the JIT (just-in-time) compiler, the part of the JVM that compiles hot bytecode to machine code while the program runs. Without it, the JVM runs every line in its bytecode interpreter. The worker stops at once. One run printed worker saw stop after 135,865,168 spins.

That flag tells you where the bug lives. It is not in the CPU cache, which is the same with or without -Xint. It is in the JIT compiler. After the loop has run many thousands of times, C2, the optimizing compiler in HotSpot (the JVM that ships with OpenJDK), turns it into machine code. C2 sees that nothing inside the loop writes stop, and nothing in the loop talks to other threads. So it reads stop once, before the loop, keeps the value in a register (a slot inside the CPU core that holds a value the code is working on), and runs the rest as while (true).

That is a legal optimization. The Java Memory Model (JMM) only promises that one thread sees another thread's write when something connects the two: a volatile field, a lock, Thread.join, and a few more you'll meet in lesson 2 of this track. A plain field has none of that, so the compiler may assume no other thread ever changes it.

The fix is one word:

Java
static volatile boolean stop;
Kotlin
@Volatile var stop = false

The JIT can't keep a volatile field in a register or move its read out of the loop. Every pass reads it again, and the JMM guarantees the write from main becomes visible.

steps: Read StopFlagDemo.java below. Predict: will the worker print worker saw stop?
Run it from labs/ with the Gradle command below. It waits 3 seconds for the worker, then exits.

Make the field static volatile boolean stop; (in the Kotlin twin, put @Volatile on stop) and run the Gradle command again.

Does it ever notice? */ public class StopFlagDemo { static boolean stop; // plain field: no volatile, no lock public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long spins = 0; while (!stop) { spins++; } System.out.printf("worker saw stop after %,d spins%n", spins); }); worker.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if the worker never stops worker.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // give the JIT time to compile the loop stop = true; System.out.println("main set stop = true"); worker.join(3_000); System.out.println("worker still running 3 s later? " + worker.isAlive()); } }

sections.h: The JIT only promises that one thread can't tell
sections.html:
Every optimizer in the JVM follows one rule, often called as-if-serial: it may change your code in any way, as long as a single thread running it alone can't tell the difference. Reading stop once is fine by that rule. If no other thread exists, stop can't change during the loop.

Here is the change C2 is allowed to make, side by side:

// what you wrote             // what the compiled code may do
while (!stop) {               if (!stop) {
    spins++;                      while (true) { spins++; }
}                             }

The same rule lets the JIT do other things you never see in one thread. It can merge two writes to the same field into one, drop a write nobody reads, or swap two writes to different fields. Each change is invisible to the thread that runs the code. Another thread, reading those fields at the same time, can see the effects.

Now the part that makes these bugs survive code review. Put almost any method call inside the loop and the hang usually goes away. A Thread.sleep(10), a log line, a Thread.yield(), even Thread.onSpinWait(). C2 treats each of these as something that may have changed memory, usually because it can't see inside the call, so it reads stop again after it.

That is luck, not a guarantee. The Java Language Specification says outright that sleep and yield have no synchronization effect, and a compiler may still read the field once. A later JDK might inline more, or a teammate might replace the log call with a counter, and the hang is back. The loop that has worked for two years is still broken. It just hasn't been compiled the wrong way yet.

So don't reason about what HotSpot does today. Ask one question: is there a synchronization point between the write and the read? For a plain field, there isn't.

try.title: Hide the bug without fixing it
steps: In StopFlagDemo (either language), remove volatile or @Volatile again so the flag is plain.
Add Thread.yield() as the first line inside the while loop. Predict before you run: will the worker stop?
Run the Gradle command from the previous Try it.
try.expect: The worker stops. Thread.yield() ends in a native call that HotSpot can't look inside, so the JIT re-reads stop after each call. The program is still incorrect by the JMM: nothing promises that re-read. Undo the change and keep volatile.

sections.h: Caches agree with each other; store buffers let a core run ahead
sections.html:
The usual story is that each CPU core keeps its own copy of stop in its cache, and the copy goes stale. That story is wrong on every server CPU you'll deploy to. Caches run a coherence protocol: when one core writes a memory location, the other cores' copies are invalidated or updated, usually within nanoseconds. No cache keeps an old value forever.

The hardware does reorder, though, through a different part of the core: the store buffer. When a core writes, it doesn't wait for the cache. It puts the write in a small queue and runs the next instruction. If the next instruction is a read of a different variable, that read can finish before the write leaves the queue. To another core, the write and the read look swapped.

The classic test for this has two threads and two fields, both starting at 0:

Java
// thread A          // thread B
x = 1;               y = 1;
r1 = y;              r2 = x;
Kotlin
// thread A          // thread B
x = 1                y = 1
r1 = y               r2 = x

In any order that keeps each thread's two lines in sequence, at least one thread reads a 1. Yet r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 happens: each thread's write is still in its own store buffer when the other thread reads. The jcstress suite measured it in 6.29% of samples on x86_64 with plain fields. With both fields volatile it never happened. The JMM forbids that outcome for volatile fields, so on x86 HotSpot follows each volatile write with an instruction that drains the store buffer before any later read.

x86 only lets a later read pass an earlier write. ARM, which runs Apple Silicon laptops and AWS Graviton servers, also lets reads pass reads and writes pass writes. Code that never fails on an x86 build agent can fail on an ARM pod.

try.title: Catch the CPU reordering
steps: Read ReorderDemo.java. It runs the two-thread test above about half a million times with plain fields, then with volatile fields.
Run it with the Gradle command below and note the counts.
Run the Java file in the interpreter: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java. Predict first: the JIT is off now, so will the plain count drop to zero?

code.title: ReorderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l01; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class ReorderDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class Volatile { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with volatile fields (of %,d)%n", run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int withVolatile() throws InterruptedException { Volatile[] s = new Volatile[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Volatile(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait for the other thread for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } }

alt.title: ReorderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l01 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class PlainPair { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class VolatilePair { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with @Volatile fields (of %,d)" .format(run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS)) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { PlainPair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun withVolatile(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { VolatilePair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() // wait for the other thread for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 }

try.expect: With plain fields a large share of trials see both reads return 0 (runs here showed between 85,000 and 330,000 of 524,288, and it changes every run). With volatile fields the count is 0 every time. Under -Xint the plain count stays high: the interpreter doesn't reorder anything, so this one is the store buffer, not the compiler.

video.title: Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register

sections.h: Three layers reorder your code, and the memory model is the contract
sections.html:
Three layers stand between your source and what other threads observe.

  • javac barely changes order. It compiles statements to bytecode almost one for one.
  • The JIT (C1, then C2 for hot code) hoists reads, merges and removes writes, and moves independent loads and stores around.
  • The CPU runs ahead through store buffers, and on ARM it reorders more freely still.

Each layer follows as-if-serial, so a single thread never notices. You can't control which layer does what, and you don't need to. The JMM is the contract that sits above all three. It names the operations that link threads: volatile reads and writes, taking and releasing a lock, thread start and join, and the classes in java.util.concurrent. If every read of shared data is linked to the write it needs by those operations, the JMM guarantees that your program behaves as if its lines ran in some single interleaved order. That property is called sequential consistency, and lesson 2 of this track shows how the links work.

If you skip the links, you have a data race, and the guarantees mostly go away. You can see a stale value, a value that seems to arrive before the write that made it, or, for long and double, half of one write and half of another.

This is why "it works on my machine" means so little here. Your test ran on one CPU family, with one JIT, under one load profile. A different JDK, a busier server or an ARM instance can expose a reordering your tests never saw. In one jcstress test, a thread writes x and then y, the compiler is told to keep that order, and another thread reads y and then x. On x86_64, seeing the new y with the old x never happened. On AArch64 (64-bit ARM) it happened in 0.68% of samples. Both results obey the same JMM. Write to the contract, and the hardware becomes someone else's problem.

Check yourself: you run StopFlagDemo with -Xint on an ARM laptop, which reorders more than x86. Does the worker stop? It does. The interpreter reads stop from memory on every pass, and coherence brings the new value to the worker's core. ARM's extra freedom only changes the order in which writes to different fields become visible. Each write still arrives. The plain field is still a data race, though, so the fix stays volatile.

analogy: Picture a cashier who checks the "store closing" sign once at the start of the shift, writes "open" on a sticky note, and from then on only looks at the note. The manager can flip the sign at 9 pm and the cashier keeps selling. That's the JIT and a register. Making the field volatile is a rule that says: look at the sign every single time. The analogy breaks on the hardware side. The store buffer is more like the manager holding the new sign for a few seconds before hanging it, while already walking on to the next task. That delay is short and always ends; the sticky note never updates.
world: Look at every background loop in your services that ends with a flag: a Kafka consumer thread with private boolean running = true and a shutdown hook that sets it to false, a Quarkus @Scheduled job that a health check pauses, a reconciliation worker that drains an in-memory batch. Most of them call poll() or do I/O inside the loop, which hides the bug on today's HotSpot. Then someone optimizes the loop to drain a local list first, the loop becomes tight, and a pod that used to stop in 200 ms hangs until Kubernetes kills it 30 seconds later. Make every cross-thread flag volatile or an AtomicBoolean, so the guarantee lives in the code and not in the JIT's mood.
mistake: The most common mistake is "fixing" a hung loop by adding Thread.sleep, a log statement or Thread.onSpinWait() to it, seeing it stop, and moving on. Each of those happens to make HotSpot re-read the field today, because the JIT can't see what the call does. None of them is a synchronization point in the JMM, and the JLS says so for sleep and yield. A future JDK or a small refactoring brings the hang back. The fix is to declare the flag volatile (or use AtomicBoolean), and keep any sleep only if you want the pause.

compare.title: A stop flag in Java and Kotlin

java.title: SettlementLoop.java
java.html: public class SettlementLoop implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { while (running) { settleNextBatch(); } } public void stop() { running = false; } }

kotlin.title: SettlementLoop.kt
kotlin.html: class SettlementLoop : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { while (running) { settleNextBatch() } } fun stop() { running = false } }

compare.note: Kotlin has no volatile keyword. You put @Volatile on a var property, and the compiler marks its JVM backing field volatile, so the bytecode is the same as the Java version. A val can't be @Volatile, because it is never written after construction. A plain Kotlin var has exactly the same bug as a plain Java field: a while (running) loop compiles to a field read the JIT can hoist. AtomicBoolean from java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same in both languages.

worked.title: Find the flags that freeze a standby pod

steps.say: Two pods run a ledger exporter, and leader election picks one of them. When the standby pod is elected, a callback thread calls onElected(). On shutdown, a hook thread calls stop(). In a failover drill the standby was elected, exported nothing, and then ignored SIGTERM until Kubernetes killed it. Find the shared state before reading on.
steps.code: class LedgerExporter implements Runnable { private boolean leader; // 1. written by the election callback thread private boolean running = true; // 2. written by the shutdown hook thread @Override public void run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a hot loop if (leader) exportBatch(); } } void onElected() { leader = true; } void stop() { running = false; } }

alt.html: class LedgerExporter : Runnable { private var leader = false // 1. written by the election callback thread private var running = true // 2. written by the shutdown hook thread override fun run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a hot loop if (leader) exportBatch() } } fun onElected() { leader = true } fun stop() { running = false } }

steps.say: Both flags are written by one thread and read by another, with nothing linking them. On the standby, leader stays false for hours, so the profile says exportBatch() never runs. C2 compiles the loop as if that branch were not there. What's left is two reads of plain fields that nothing in the loop writes, so C2 reads them once. A copy of this class run for this lesson exported 0 batches after onElected() and was still spinning 3 seconds after stop().
Make both flags volatile. Then stop the standby from spinning: it has nothing to do, so it should sleep between checks and leave the core to other work.
steps.code: class LedgerExporter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean leader; // 1. both flags cross threads: both volatile private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { try { while (running) { // 2. re-read on every pass if (leader) { exportBatch(); } else { Thread.sleep(50); // 3. a standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } void onElected() { leader = true; } void stop() { running = false; } }

alt.html: class LedgerExporter : Runnable { @Volatile private var leader = false // 1. both flags cross threads: both @Volatile @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { try { while (running) { // 2. re-read on every pass if (leader) { exportBatch() } else { Thread.sleep(50) // 3. a standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } fun onElected() { leader = true } fun stop() { running = false } }

steps.say: The sleep alone would also have hidden the hang, because HotSpot re-reads fields after it. That is why the volatile stays. The sleep is there to save CPU. The volatile is there for correctness, and it keeps working after the next refactoring.

lab.title: Unhang a settlement loop and a rate board
steps: Run the tests once. Two of the three fail with "still spinning" or "still waiting". Each failing test waits 5 seconds for a thread that never finishes, so the run takes a little while.
Fix SettlementLoop with the smallest change that makes the write in stop() reach the loop. Run the tests.
In FxRateBoard, first try making only rates volatile and run the tests. Predict whether it passes, then see.
Now fix the field that matters. Leave the other one plain. Run the tests three times in a row.
hints: The tests sleep 300 ms before calling stop() or publish(). That gives the JIT time to compile the spinning loop, which is when the plain field gets read once and never again.
awaitRates() spins on ready, not on rates. The field the loop reads is the one the JIT can hoist.
Why may rates stay plain? It is written before the volatile write to ready, and read after the volatile read sees true. Lesson 2 of this track names that rule.
Adding Thread.onSpinWait() or a log call to the loop may make a test pass on HotSpot. That is the accident from section 2. Fix the field instead.
lab.done: All three tests in VisibilityTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A worker that is sure to stop
drill.prompt: Close this page. From memory, write a class Poller implements Runnable whose run() loops calling pollOnce() until another thread calls shutdown(). It must be guaranteed to stop. Then write one sentence on why a plain boolean is not enough.

answer.html: public class Poller implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; // volatile: the loop re-reads it, the write is visible @Override public void run() { while (running) { pollOnce(); } } public void shutdown() { running = false; } private void pollOnce() { /* fetch and handle one batch */ } } // With a plain boolean, nothing links the write in shutdown() to the read in run(), // so the JIT may read the field once and loop forever.

alt.html: class Poller : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true // @Volatile: the loop re-reads it, the write is visible override fun run() { while (running) { pollOnce() } } fun shutdown() { running = false } private fun pollOnce() { /* fetch and handle one batch */ } } // With a plain var, nothing links the write in shutdown() to the read in run(), // so the JIT may read the field once and loop forever.

recap: A loop on a plain field can spin forever: the JIT may read the field once and keep it in a register.
The hang goes away under -Xint, which proves it comes from the compiler, not from CPU caches.
Caches are coherent. Store buffers let a core's later read pass its own earlier write, which reorders what other threads see.
Every layer (javac, JIT, CPU) may reorder as long as one thread alone can't tell. Other threads can tell.
sleep, yield, log lines and onSpinWait hide the bug on today's HotSpot but guarantee nothing. Use volatile or an atomic.
Correctness comes from the JMM, not from your CPU: code that passes on x86 can fail on ARM.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "The shutdown flag works when I step through it in the debugger, so it can't be a visibility bug." Explain, in your own words, why it hangs in production and what the fix is.
explain.answer: In the debugger the code runs slowly and often interpreted, so every pass of the loop reads the field from memory and sees the new value. In production the loop gets hot, the JIT compiles it, and because the field is plain and nothing in the loop synchronizes, the compiler is allowed to read it once and keep the value in a register. The CPU caches are not the problem; they stay in sync. The fix is to make the flag volatile (or an AtomicBoolean). Then the JIT must read it on every pass, and the memory model guarantees the write from the shutdown thread becomes visible.

deeper.html:
volatile is the usual fix, but it does more than this loop needs. The weakest mode that already guarantees the loop ends is opaque access through a VarHandle (getOpaque and setOpaque, JDK 9+). The jcstress sample BasicJMM_04_Progress makes the point: the plain spin loop is marked "Test is stuck" as an allowed outcome, while for both the volatile and the opaque spin loops getting stuck is forbidden. Opaque stops the compiler from caching the read and leaves the hardware's own guarantee (writes become visible eventually) in place. It does not order other fields, which is why it's rarely what you want. Lesson 6 of this track covers the modes.

The jcstress sample BasicJMM_06_Causality is the cleanest look at hardware differences. One thread writes x = 1 then y = 1, and another reads y then x. With plain fields, the sample's recorded run saw y == 1 but x == 0 in 0.09% of samples. With opaque accesses, which keep the compiler from reordering, x86_64 showed it 0 times, because x86 keeps stores in order. An AArch64 machine still showed it in 0.68% of samples. Make y volatile and the outcome is forbidden on every platform.

If you want the long version of why the JMM is written as a contract over executions, read Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics". It is long, and worth one slow evening.
